topics.title: Seats and blinds
topics.short: The six seats at the table, the two blinds that must be posted, and the order in which everyone acts.

simple.text: A six-player table has six seats with fixed names. The **button** (BTN) is the dealer. The two seats after it put in forced bets before anyone sees a card: the **small blind** (SB) posts 0.5 and the **big blind** (BB) posts 1. The other three seats are **under the gun** (UTG), the **hijack** (HJ) and the **cutoff** (CO).

head: Seat
Short
Acts before the flop
Acts after the flop
simple.caption: Only the players still in the hand act, but the order never changes.

simple.text: All amounts on this site are in **big blinds** (bb). Everyone starts with 100 bb, so a 5 bb pot is 5% of a stack.
Acting last is an advantage: you see what the others did before you decide. That is why the late seats open far more hands than UTG. See [[position]].

deeper.text: Why the blinds matter

Before anyone acts there is already 1.5 bb in the middle. Every opening raise is partly an attempt to win that dead money, and the fewer players are left behind you, the more often you win it straight away. That is the main reason the later seats open more hands ([[preflop-charts]]).
Order of action

items: Before the flop: UTG, HJ, CO, BTN, SB, BB. The big blind acts last because its blind already counts as a bet.
After the flop: SB, BB, UTG, HJ, CO, BTN. The button acts last on every street.

deeper.title: The most common pot on this site: button opens, big blind calls
deeper.result: Pot on the flop: 5.5 bb, with 100 - 2.5 = 97.5 bb behind for each player.

deeper.text: Do not mix up the two orders. The small blind is fifth to act before the flop but **first** after it, so it plays every postflop street [[position|out of position]].
Every puzzle on this site is heads-up after the flop. The player who acts last is called **IP** (in position), the one who acts first **OOP** (out of position).

Everyone folds to the small blind, which raises to 3. The big blind calls. This is called **blind against blind**.

check.why: After the flop the order is SB, BB, then the other seats, with the button always last. The preflop raise does not change the order; the big blind checks or bets first.

check.q: UTG raises to 2.5, everyone folds to the big blind, who calls. How big is the pot on the flop?
check.why: 2.5 from UTG, 2.5 from the big blind and the small blind's 0.5, which stays in the pot after it folds: 5.5 bb. Answering 5 forgets the small blind's dead 0.5.

topics.title: Hand names and the 13x13 grid
topics.short: How hands are written (AKs suited, AKo offsuit, 77 a pair) and how the 169 kinds of starting hand fill the 13x13 grid.

simple.text: A starting hand is two cards. Write the two ranks, highest first, then **s** if the cards share a suit (suited) or **o** if they do not (offsuit). T stands for ten.

simple.caption: Ace-king of hearts is written AKs: ace-king suited.

simple.text: {Ah}{Kd} is AKo, ace-king offsuit. {7s}{7c} is 77, a pocket pair; pairs need no letter.

If you ignore which exact suits you hold, there are only **169** kinds of starting hand: 13 pairs, 78 suited hands and 78 offsuit hands. The site lays them out in a 13 by 13 grid: pairs on the diagonal, suited hands above it, offsuit hands below it.
Suited is up and to the right, offsuit is down and to the left. AKs sits in row A, column K; AKo in row K, column A.

deeper.text: How many ways each hand can be dealt
Each exact pair of cards is called a **combo**. Different kinds of hand have different numbers of combos:

deeper.text: Families of hands

items: **Broadways**: both cards T or higher (AK, KQ, QJ, JT and so on).
**Suited connectors**: suited, ranks next to each other (98s, 65s). **Suited gappers** skip one rank (97s, 86s).
**Suited aces**: A2s to AKs. A5s to A2s are also called wheel aces, because they can make the lowest straight, A-2-3-4-5 (the **wheel**).
**Pocket pairs**: small (22 to 66), medium (77 to TT) and big (JJ and up).

deeper.text: "AK" with no letter means all 16 combos. In a chart, AKs and AKo are different cells and can have different strategies.

check.why: JTo has 12 combos and JTs only 4, so JTo turns up three times as often. Each exact pair of cards is equally likely; there are simply more offsuit pairs.

check.why: Four aces, choose two: 4 x 3 / 2 = 6. Four is the count for a suited hand, twelve for an offsuit hand.

topics.title: Open, call, 3-bet, 4-bet
topics.short: The preflop moves: the opening raise, the call, the re-raise (3-bet) and the raise after that (4-bet).

simple.text: Before the flop each player can fold, call or raise. Players count the raises: the big blind is the first bet, so the first raise is the **open**, a re-raise is a **3-bet**, and a raise of the 3-bet is a **4-bet**.
When the big blind calls or 3-bets an open, players say it **defends**. Each move tells the others something about your [[range]]: a 3-bet shows a stronger (or a bluffing) range than a call.
Fold, call and raise are the only three things you can do. The chart for a spot tells you which one each hand takes.

deeper.text: 3-bets are bigger out of position (11 from the big blind, about 4.4 times the open) than in position (8.5 from the button, 3.4 times). The player without position needs a bigger pot to compensate for acting first on every later street.
Two kinds of 3-bet

items: **Value 3-bets**: hands that want a bigger pot because they are ahead of the opener's calling range, such as TT+, AK and AQ against a button open.
**Bluff 3-bets**: hands that are not good enough to call but have useful [[blockers]] and can still make strong hands, such as A5s, which the big blind 3-bets every time against a button open.
The hands in between usually **call**: they play well after the flop but do not want to build a big pot.

deeper.text: Calling from the small blind is rare in modern charts: the big blind is still behind you and can squeeze (3-bet after an open and a call). On this site the SB against a BTN open only 3-bets or folds.

examples.text: Example 1: the pot after a 3-bet
The button opens to 2.5, the small blind folds, the big blind 3-bets to 11 and the button calls.

examples.result: Pot 22.5 bb, 89 bb behind each: a 3-bet pot is four times bigger than the 5.5 bb pot after a call.

examples.text: Example 2: your turn
The small blind opens to 3, the big blind 3-bets to 9, the small blind calls. Pot?

examples.result: 9 + 9 = 18: pot 18 bb, 91 bb behind each.

check.q: The cutoff opens, the button re-raises. What is the button's move called?
check.why: The big blind counts as the first bet and the cutoff's open as the second, so the button's re-raise is the 3-bet. A 4-bet would be the cutoff raising again.

check.q: Why does the big blind 3-bet to 11 but the button only to 8.5?
options: The big blind has more chips
The player out of position wants a bigger pot to make up for acting first
check.why: Acting first on every later street is a handicap, so out-of-position 3-bets are larger and take the opener's weaker hands out. Stacks are equal, so chip count is not the reason.

topics.title: Made hands: pairs, kickers, sets
topics.short: The names for what you have after the flop: top pair, overpair, kicker, set, two pair, the nuts.

simple.text: A **made hand** is one that already has something: a pair or better. The names say which board card you paired.

simple.caption: Top pair (kings) with a jack kicker.

items: **Top pair**: you pair the highest board card. **Second** (middle) and **bottom pair**: the lower ones.
**Kicker**: your other card. It decides who wins when both players have the same pair.
**Overpair**: a pocket pair above every board card, like QQ on J-8-3. An **underpair** is below them.
**Set**: a pocket pair that matched a board card (77 on K-7-2). **Trips**: one card in hand plus a pair on the board.
**The nuts**: the best possible hand on that board.

simple.text: Name your hand, then ask what it beats. "Top pair, jack kicker" loses to every king with a better kicker.

deeper.text: Hand ranks, strongest first
Only your best five cards count. A kicker matters only when the five cards would otherwise tie.
Domination
A hand is **dominated** when it shares a card with a better hand: KQ against AK on a king-high board. The worse hand has very few ways to win, because pairing its shared card does not help.
Top pair is not automatically strong. Against a player who only continues with good kings, a weak kicker is often behind. Ask what calls or raises you, not just what you hold.

Sets are much stronger than trips, because a set is hidden: with 77 on K-7-2 nobody expects you to have a seven. With trips (A7 on 7-7-2) a second 7 in the other player's hand would tie or beat you on kickers.

topics.title: Draws: flush, straight, gutshot, backdoor
topics.short: A draw is a hand that is not good yet but can become very strong with the right card on the turn or river.

simple.text: A **draw** is a hand that needs one more good card. You count the cards that complete it; those are your [[outs]].

simple.caption: A flush draw: four hearts, nine more hearts in the deck.

head: Draw
What you need
Outs
rows: one more card of your suit
either end of four in a row

simple.text: Draws are best played aggressively: a bet with a draw can win the pot right away and still has outs when called. That is a [[bluff|semi-bluff]].

deeper.text: The common draws

items: **Flush draw**: four cards of one suit. 13 cards in a suit, 4 seen, so 9 left.
**Open-ended straight draw**: four in a row with both ends open, like 9-8 on T-7-2: any jack or six makes a straight, 2 x 4 = 8 outs.
**Gutshot**: one card missing inside, like Q-9 on K-J-4: only a ten works, 4 outs.
**Double gutshot**: two different inside cards work, 8 outs, as good as open-ended.
**Combo draw**: flush draw plus straight draw, often 12 to 15 outs. With that many outs you can be the favourite even against top pair.
**Backdoor draw**: you need **two** running cards, turn and river, such as three to a flush on the flop.

deeper.title: How often a backdoor flush comes in
deeper.result: 4.2%: small, but it adds up with other small extras, which is why the solver keeps betting some backdoor hands.

deeper.text: The nut flush draw
A flush draw with the ace of that suit is the **nut flush draw**: if it comes in you have the best possible flush. Smaller flush draws can complete and still lose to a bigger flush.
Not every out is clean. If your flush card also pairs the board, an opponent with a set makes a full house. Counting properly is in [[equity-calc]].

check.why: Any jack (J-T-9-8-7) or any six (T-9-8-7-6) makes a straight: two ranks x 4 cards = 8. Four would be a gutshot, nine a flush draw.

check.why: Both have nine outs, but {Ah}{5h} draws to the nut flush. With {6h}{5h} a heart can also give an opponent with a bigger heart a better flush.

topics.title: In position and out of position
topics.short: Being in position means acting last after the flop: you see the other player's move before you choose yours.

simple.text: Think of a card game where you always get to see your friend's move before you make yours. That is **position**. The player who acts last after the flop is **in position** (IP); the other is **out of position** (OOP).
On this site the button is in position against the blinds, and the big blind is in position only against the small blind.

simple.caption: With a gutshot in position you can check behind and see the turn for free; out of position you never know if a check will be followed by a bet.

simple.text: Position is worth chips on every street. Play more hands when you will be in position, fewer when you will not.

deeper.text: What position gives you

items: **Information**: you see a check or a bet before you choose.
**Free cards**: when the other player checks, you can check behind and see the next card without paying.
**Control of the pot size**: the last player decides whether a street is checked through.
**Equity realisation**: your hand wins closer to its fair share. Out of position you often have to fold a hand with some [[equity]] because you face bets you cannot call.

deeper.text: **Realising equity** means actually winning your share. A hand with 35% equity that has to fold to a bet on the turn realises less than 35%; the same hand in position, getting free cards, realises more.

Do not judge a preflop call by equity alone. A hand with 40% equity out of position may be a fold, while the same hand in position is a call, because the out-of-position hand will realise less of its equity.
How the site shows it
Each puzzle labels the hero IP or OOP. When the out-of-position player 'checks (forced)' on the flop, it is because the bet sizes chosen for that pot do not let the caller lead (see [[lines]]).

The button opens half as many again, because only the blinds are left and it will play the rest of the hand in position against them. The big blind defends wide against the button for a different reason: it already has 1 bb in the pot, so the price is good.

topics.title: Range
topics.short: A range is every hand a player could have in a spot, with how often they would play each one that way.

simple.text: You never know the other player's two cards. But you do know what they did, and that rules hands in and out. The list of hands they could hold is their **range**.

Example: a careful friend raises first from under the gun. They would not do that with {7c}{2d}, but they would with {As}{Ks}. Write down everything they would raise with, and that is their UTG range: on this site, 17.6% of all hands.

simple.title: UTG opening range
simple.caption: Coloured cells are hands UTG raises. A partly filled cell is raised only that share of the time, for example 66 about 65%.

simple.text: Every action narrows the range. After the flop, a player who bets big usually has a strong hand or a draw; a player who checks usually has fewer strong hands.
Put the other player on a range, never on one hand. Then ask: how much of that range am I beating?

deeper.text: Ranges have weights

A range is not just a list. Each hand class has a **weight**: the share of its combos that are in the range. In the UTG chart above, 66 has weight 64.6% (3.9 of its 6 combos), K8s 89.2% and 87s 21.2%. These are the solver's real mixing frequencies, which is why they are not round numbers. The size of a range is counted in [[combos]].

deeper.text: How a range narrows

items: Preflop: the chart for the seat and the action (open, call, 3-bet).
Flop: the cards on the board remove combos (no one can hold the ace of spades if it is on the board) and each check, bet or raise keeps only the hands that would do that.
By the river, a range that bet three times is mostly very strong hands and missed draws.

deeper.text: On the play screen, **Your range** and **Villain's range** show the ranges arriving at the current decision (see [[reading-charts]]).
"He must have aces" is the classic mistake. Even when one hand is likely, the rest of the range decides whether calling or betting makes money.

Your own hand is also part of a range. The other player cannot see your cards either; they face your range. That is why the solver sometimes plays a hand in a surprising way: the hand is doing a job for the whole range ([[gto]]).

UTG's range is full of AK, AQ, KQ and big pairs that dominate KJ. The button's range has many weaker hands, so KJ is ahead of it.

check.q: A tight player raises from UTG. You hold {Kh}{Jd}. Why is it weaker here than against a button raise?
options: UTG's range contains many hands that dominate KJ, like AK, AQ and KQ
KJ is never a good hand
check.why: Against the UTG range KJ has about 42% equity, against the button range about 52%. Same cards, different range. UTG does not always have aces; their range simply has more hands that beat KJ.

check.q: What does a half-filled cell in a range chart mean?
options: Half of that hand's combos are in the range
check.why: The fill height is the weight: the share of that hand's combos still in the range. It says nothing about strength or suits.

topics.title: Counting combos
topics.short: A combo is one exact two-card hand; counting them tells you how likely each part of a range is.

simple.text: Not all hands are equally likely. There are 6 ways to be dealt a pair, 4 ways for a suited hand and 12 for an offsuit one. Each way is a **combo**.
Cards you can see change the count. If a king is on the board, only 3 kings are left, so KK drops from 6 combos to 3.

simple.caption: You hold an ace, so the other player has fewer ace-king combos.

simple.text: 6 for a pair, 4 suited, 12 offsuit. Then take away any card you can see.

deeper.text: The formulas

items: Pair, with n cards of that rank left: n x (n - 1) / 2. Four left: 6. Three left: 3. Two left: 1.
Unpaired hand: (cards left of rank 1) x (cards left of rank 2). Of those, the suited combos are the suits both ranks still have.

deeper.title: Combos in the example above (board {Ks}{7d}{2c}, you hold {Ah}{Qh})

steps.label: AK
steps.value: 3 aces left x 3 kings left = 9 (it would be 4 x 3 = 12 without your ace)

deeper.result: Sets: 9 combos. AK: 9 combos. Without your ace AK would be 12, so your card removes a quarter of them.

deeper.text: That effect of your own cards is called card removal or [[blockers]].
Do not count "hands" as if each class were one. "He has a set or AK" sounds like 4 hands against 1, but in the example it is 9 combos against 9.

topics.title: Blockers
topics.short: Holding a card means the other player cannot hold it. A blocker makes some of their hands less likely.

simple.text: There is only one ace of hearts in the deck. If it is in your hand, it is not in anyone else's. That is a **blocker**.

simple.caption: Nobody else can have the best possible flush: you hold the ace of hearts.

simple.text: Blockers rarely matter for what you hold; they matter for what you **pretend** to hold and for what you call. A bluff works better when your cards make the other player's strong hands less likely.
When you bluff, hold the cards that block their calls and do not block their folds. When you call, hold the cards that block their value hands.

deeper.text: Two classic blocker plays

items: **Bluff 3-bets with hands like A5s**: the ace makes AA, AK and AQ less likely, so the opener has fewer hands that can continue. The hand can still make a straight or a flush when called.
**River bluffs with the nut-flush blocker**: on a three-flush board, holding the ace of that suit means the other player cannot have the nut flush.

deeper.title: Flushes on a monotone board, {Kh}{9h}{4h}

steps.label: Two-heart combos the other player can hold
Combos with the ace of hearts

deeper.result: Your {Ah} removes 9 of 45 flush combos (20%), including every nut flush.

deeper.text: Unblocking

The reverse matters too. If you bluff while holding cards that the other player's **folding** hands need, you leave them with more calling hands. A missed flush draw is a bad bluff when the other player's missed flush draws would fold: you block those folds.
Blockers are a tie-breaker, not a reason on their own. Deciding to bluff with a blocker only makes sense when the bet already makes sense for your range.

examples.text: Example 1: blocking value on the river

Board {Kd}{Td}{6s}{3c}{2h}, villain bets. You hold {Kc}{9c}. Your {Kc} removes one king, so KT (two pair) drops from 9 combos to 6. Your {9c} removes the club combos of Q9s and J9s, the bluffs. Net effect, counted in [[combos]]: 12 value combos against 10 bluffs.
Example 2: your turn
Board {Qh}{Jh}{4c}{2s}{8d}. The heart draw missed. You want to bluff. Which hand blocks fewer of villain's folding hands: {Ah}{3c} or {As}{3c}?
Answer: {As}{3c}. Villain's missed heart draws would fold, and {Ah} removes some of them (every combo with the ace of hearts). {As} leaves all those folds in their range.

check.q: You hold {As}. How many AK combos can the opponent have if no ace or king is on the board?
check.why: Your ace leaves 3 aces x 4 kings = 12. Blockers do not remove a hand completely; they shrink it.

check.q: The flush draw missed on the river. Which makes a better bluff?
options: A hand that holds a card of the missed flush suit
A hand with no card of that suit
check.why: Villain's missed flush draws are the hands that fold to a bluff. Holding a card of that suit removes some of those folds, so the bluff is called more often by hands that beat you.

topics.title: Range advantage and nut advantage
topics.short: Range advantage: your whole range has more equity on this board. Nut advantage: you have more of the very best hands.

simple.text: Imagine two teams, each holding a whole range of hands. When the flop comes, one team usually has more good hands than the other. That team has the **range advantage**.

simple.caption: Ace-high boards favour the preflop raiser: they open more aces and strong hands than the caller keeps.

simple.text: Using this site's charts, on {Ac}{Td}{4s} the button's opening range has 56% equity against the big blind's calling range. Against an early-position range it is even more lopsided: UTG's range has 63%.
The player with the range advantage can bet small with almost everything. The player with the nut advantage can bet big.

deeper.text: Two different edges

items: **Range advantage** is about the average: total [[equity]] of your range against theirs. The site shows it as the equity bar on the range view: "Your range 58%, Villain 42%".
**Nut advantage** is about the top: who has more sets, two pairs, straights and flushes. A range can be ahead on average and still have fewer nuts.

deeper.text: Why it decides the c-bet

With a range advantage, betting a small amount with the whole range is cheap and makes the other range's weak hands fold. With a nut advantage you can bet large, because the other player cannot have many hands that beat you. Both ideas are in [[sizing]] and [[c-bet]].

topics.title: Polarised, merged and capped ranges
topics.short: A polarised range is very strong hands plus bluffs; a merged range is mostly medium hands; a capped range has no very strong hands.

simple.text: Picture a range as a line from the worst hand to the best. A **polarised** range takes only the two ends: monsters and bluffs, nothing in the middle. A **merged** (linear) range takes the top chunk: strong and medium hands, few bluffs.
Big bets come from polarised ranges, small bets from merged ones. When someone bets big, ask: which monsters and which bluffs?

deeper.text: Why the shape decides the size

A medium hand does not want to bet big: worse hands fold and better hands call. So a big bet only makes sense for hands that are happy either way, the nuts (called by worse) and bluffs (which win only when the other player folds). That is a polarised range. A small bet can include medium hands, because worse hands still call it.
Capped ranges

A range is **capped** when it cannot contain the strongest hands. Example from this site's charts: the big blind's **calling** range against a button open contains no TT or better, no AK, no AQs and almost no AQo (3%), because those hands 3-bet. So on {Ah}{Qd}{Tc} the big blind cannot have AA, QQ or TT and almost never has AK or AQ, while the button can have all of them.

deeper.title: Big blind calling range against a button open
deeper.caption: The top-left corner (big pairs, AK, AQ) is empty or nearly empty: those hands 3-bet instead.

deeper.text: Do not bet big with a medium hand just because you think you are ahead. If only better hands call, the big bet turns your medium hand into a bluff.

examples.text: Example: the river

Board {Qc}{8d}{5s}{3c}{2h}. You have {Qh}{Jd}, top pair with a good kicker. A big overbet is called mainly by hands that beat you, such as AQ, KQ and sets; a half-pot bet can also be called by worse queens like QT and Q9. Your hand belongs in a **merged** betting range with a small size (worked out in [[value]]).
Your turn

Your betting range on the river is only nut flushes and missed straight draws, with no medium hands. Which size fits: small or large? Answer: large. Nothing in your betting range needs a small size, and a large bet gets more from the flushes and more folds from the bluffs.

check.q: Which range is polarised?
check.why: Polarised means both ends of the line: the strongest hands and hands that cannot win at showdown. Top and second pairs are medium hands, a merged range.

check.q: Why is the big blind's calling range capped against a button open on this site?
options: Its best hands (TT+, AK, AQ) 3-bet instead of calling
check.why: In the BB_vs_BTN chart TT+, AKs, AQs and AKo are 3-bets every time and AQo 97% of the time, so the calling range has almost none of them. The calling range still has many pairs, such as 22 to 88.

topics.title: Mixed strategies and frequencies
topics.short: Why the solver says "bet 60%, check 40%": when two actions earn the same, playing both keeps you unpredictable.

simple.text: Think of rock-paper-scissors. If you always play rock, your friend wins every time with paper. The unbeatable plan is to mix: each one a third of the time. Poker works the same way.

When the site shows **Bet 60% / Check 40%** for your hand, it means: in this exact spot, the solver bets this hand 60% of the time and checks it 40%. Both actions earn (almost) the same; mixing them keeps your range balanced.

If the solver mixes, both choices are fine. On this site any action the solver takes at least 3.5% of the time is graded Correct or Best, and after the flop so is any action that costs at most 0.2% of the pot.

deeper.text: Indifference: why EVs are tied

A solver only mixes when the actions have the same [[ev|expected value]]. If betting were better, it would always bet. So a mix means the hand is **indifferent**: you lose nothing by picking either action. Explanations on this site often say the options are "tied" for this reason.
How a mix turns into points

deeper.title: Solver: bet 60%, check 40%. You check.
deeper.result: Grade Correct, 87 points. Betting would be Best, 100 points. The full rules are in [[reading-feedback]].

deeper.text: Range frequencies and hand frequencies

Two different numbers appear on the screen. The **action buttons** show the frequency for **your hand**. The bar above the range grid shows how the **whole range** splits: "Bet 58%" there means 58% of all the combos in the range bet.
Do not try to copy a 60/40 mix with a coin flip at the table. What matters is that the range as a whole bets the right amount; picking either action with a mixed hand is fine.

examples.text: Example: reading a mix

Suppose the buttons after your pick show Check 5%, Bet a third 90%, Bet three quarters 5%. Betting a third is the main play; the other two are rare. If you checked, your frequency 0.05 is above 0.035 but far below the top, so it is Correct with 60 + 40 x 0.05 / 0.90 = 62 points.
Your turn
Buttons show Call 50%, Raise 48%, Fold 2%. You raise. Grade? Answer: Best, because 0.48 >= 0.50 - 0.05. You score 100.

check.q: The solver bets your hand 55% and checks it 45%. What does that tell you about the EV of the two actions?
check.why: A solver mixes only when the actions earn the same. The percentages describe how often, not how much better. Neither is a mistake.

check.q: Your hand on the turn: Fold 2%, Call 98%. You fold, and folding costs 0.03 bb in a 20 bb pot. What grade?
check.why: Below 3.5% the frequency no longer decides, the EV loss does: 0.03 / 20 = 0.15% of the pot. At most 0.2% is still Correct; under 1.5% would be Inaccuracy, under 6% Wrong, more Blunder.

topics.title: GTO and the solver
topics.short: GTO is a strategy that cannot be beaten in the long run; a solver is the program that calculates it.

simple.text: **GTO** (game theory optimal) is a way of playing that no opponent can beat in the long run, whatever they do. It does not try to read your friends; it plays so that reading it does not help.
A **solver** is a computer program that finds that strategy for a given spot by playing against itself millions of times and fixing its own weaknesses. Every answer on this site comes from a solver.
GTO is the safe baseline. Against a friend who never bluffs, you can fold more than GTO says; that is an exploit, and it can be beaten back if they change.

deeper.text: What the solver on this site does

items: It knows both ranges at the start of the flop (from this site's preflop charts), the stacks, and a fixed menu of bet sizes for each street.
It finds, for every hand in both ranges, how often to take each option so that neither player can gain by changing.
It stops when the strategy is within a small margin of perfect, measured as exploitability: a fraction of a percent of the pot.

deeper.text: Limits worth knowing

items: The preflop charts come from a published preflop solver solution (6-max, 100 bb, 2.5x opens, NL500 rake); they were not solved by this site. Their odd-looking percentages, like 64.6%, are real mixing frequencies. After the flop the site solves without rake.
Only a few bet sizes exist in each spot (for example a third or three quarters of the pot on the flop). Real players can use any size.
The solver assumes a perfect opponent. Against real people, the best play can differ.

deeper.text: **Balanced** means a range has the right mix of value hands and bluffs for its bet size, so the opponent cannot profit by always calling or always folding (see [[bluff-catcher]]).
GTO is not "always bet" or "always the same". It is often a mix, and it changes with every board and size ([[frequencies]]).

examples.text: Example: exploiting a friend

A pot-size river bet needs 33% equity to call. The GTO bettor bluffs just often enough (one bluff for every two value bets) that your bluff catcher breaks even. If your friend never bluffs, every call loses: you should fold all your bluff catchers. That is an exploit. If he finds out and starts bluffing every time, you switch back.
Example 2: a balanced betting range
You bet half the pot on the river with 12 combos of value. How many bluffs make the caller indifferent?

steps.label: Bluff share for a half-pot bet

examples.result: 12 value + 4 bluffs. With more bluffs the caller should always call; with fewer, always fold.

examples.text: Your turn
Same 12 value combos, but you bet the size of the pot. How many bluffs now? (Answer: bluffs are a third of the range, 2 value per bluff: 6 bluffs. Bigger bets can carry more bluffs.)

check.q: What does GTO guarantee?
options: That no opponent strategy beats you in the long run
That you make the most money against weak players
check.why: GTO cannot be exploited. It does not win every hand, and against weak players a strategy that targets their mistakes can win more.

check.q: The solver mixes your hand 50/50. A friend says: "so the solver does not know". Is that right?
options: No: both actions earn the same, and the mix keeps the range balanced
check.why: The mix is the answer, not uncertainty. Both actions have the same EV for this hand, and the frequencies make the whole range hard to play against.

check.q: You bet pot with 10 value combos and 10 bluffs. What should a GTO-minded caller do with a bluff catcher?
options: Always call: half your bets are bluffs, more than the 33% needed
Call a third of the time
check.why: Against a pot-size bet a bluff catcher needs 33% bluffs. 50% is far more, so calling earns money. A balanced range would have about 5 bluffs, not 10.

topics.title: Equity
topics.short: Your share of the pot if the hand were played to the river many times with no more betting: 40% equity wins 40% of the time.

simple.text: Imagine you could deal the rest of the cards a thousand times and nobody bets again. **Equity** is the share of those deals you would win. Ties count as half.

simple.caption: Aces against kings before the flop: aces win about 81 times out of 100.

simple.text: So aces have 81% equity and kings 19%. If the pot is 10 bb, aces' fair share is 8.1 bb.
On the play screen, equity appears in two places: your **hand's** equity in the explanation ("88% equity"), and the **range** equity bar ("Your range 54%, Villain 46%", see [[range-advantage]]).
Equity is "how often I win if it goes to showdown", not "am I ahead right now". A flush draw is behind but can have close to 40%.

deeper.text: Equity against a range

In real hands you never face one hand but a [[range]]. Your equity against a range is the average of your equity against each combo in it, weighted by how many combos there are. The method is worked out step by step in [[equity-calc]].
Equity is not the same as winnings

Equity assumes no more betting. Real hands have more betting, so a hand can win more or less than its equity: position, initiative and how easily the hand can be played all matter ([[position]], [[implied-odds]]). The money a decision earns is its [[ev]].
"I had 70% equity so I should get it all in" is not always right. The question is what the other player's **calling** range is; against that range your equity can be much lower.

topics.title: Outs
topics.short: Outs are the unseen cards that would turn your hand into the winner.

simple.text: You are behind and need help. Each card left in the deck that would give you the best hand is an **out**.

simple.caption: Four hearts: nine more hearts in the deck, so nine outs.

simple.text: Count outs, then turn them into a percentage with the [[equity-calc|rule of 4 and 2]].

deeper.text: How to count

items: Start from what you need (a flush, a straight, a pair of your overcards).
Count the cards that make it that you cannot see: 13 of a suit minus the ones in your hand and on the board.
Do not count a card twice. With a flush draw and a straight draw, the straight cards of your suit are already among the flush outs.
Remove or discount **dirty outs**: cards that make your hand but also improve the other player to something better.

deeper.text: Clean and dirty outs
A **clean** out wins for sure. A **dirty** (tainted) out makes your hand but may not win: a heart that pairs the board when the other player has a set gives them a full house.

topics.short: Outs x 4 on the flop and outs x 2 on the turn give your rough equity; against a range, average over its combos.

simple.text: Counting outs is half the job. To turn outs into a percentage there is a simple trick:

items: On the **flop**, with two cards to come: outs x 4.
On the **turn**, with one card to come: outs x 2.

simple.caption: 9 outs on the flop: 9 x 4 = 36%. On the turn: 9 x 2 = 18%.

simple.text: Rule of 4 and 2. With more than 8 outs on the flop, subtract the extra: 15 outs is 15 x 4 - (15 - 8) = 53%.

topics.title: Pot odds: the equity you need to call
topics.short: Pot odds compare the cost of a call with the pot you can win; they tell you the equity you need to call.

simple.text: Someone offers you a bet: pay 1, and if you win you get 3 back in total. You need to win at least 1 time in 3 for that to be worth it. That is **pot odds**.

simple.title: Facing a half-pot bet
simple.result: Call when your equity is above 25%.

simple.text: Equity needed = what you call / the pot after you call.

deeper.text: The table worth learning
Using the numbers on this screen
The site's **pot** already includes the opponent's bet. So the formula on screen is: needed = to call / (pot shown + to call). If the pot shows 30 and you must call 10: 10 / 40 = 25%.
Do not divide by the pot before the bet, and do not forget your own call. 5 / 10 = 50% would be wrong; the pot you win is 20.
Pot odds tell you the **minimum**. Out of position or with a hand that will face more bets you need more; with [[implied-odds]] (money you can still win later) you can call with less.

topics.title: Expected value (EV)
topics.short: EV is what a decision wins or loses on average, in bb, if you made it many times.

simple.text: A friend offers a game: flip a coin, heads you win 3 bb, tails you lose 2 bb. You will not win every time, but on average you make (3 - 2) / 2 = 0.5 bb per flip. That average is the **expected value**, EV.
Every poker decision has an EV: fold, call, check, bet. The solver works out each one for your hand, and the best decision is the one with the highest EV.
On this site, after your pick each button shows how much less than the best option it earns, for example "-1.3 bb". That is your **EV loss**.
Judge decisions by EV, not by results. A good call that loses this time is still a good call.

deeper.text: How to calculate EV
List the possible outcomes, multiply each by its chance, add them up.

topics.title: Implied odds
topics.short: Implied odds count the money you expect to win on later streets when your draw comes in, not just the pot now.

simple.text: Sometimes a call looks too expensive for the pot today, but if you hit you will win much more later. That future money is your **implied odds**.

simple.caption: An open-ended straight draw. If a four or nine comes, the other player's king may pay you off.

simple.text: **Reverse implied odds** are the opposite: when you hit, you sometimes still lose a big pot, like a small flush against a bigger flush.
Implied odds are biggest when your draw is hidden and the other player has a strong hand that will keep paying.

items: Deep stacks give more implied odds; low [[spr]] gives few.
Obvious draws get paid less: when the third flush card comes, everyone sees it.
Draws to the nuts have implied odds; draws to second-best hands have reverse implied odds.

deeper.text: Implied odds are not a licence to call everything. If the other player will fold when you hit, there are no implied odds at all.

check.why: A flush to the six loses to almost every other flush. The money you win when it holds can be less than the money you lose when it does not.

topics.title: Minimum defence frequency (MDF)
topics.short: MDF is the share of your range you must continue with so that an opponent cannot profit by bluffing with any two cards.

simple.text: If you always fold to a bet, the other player can bet every hand and win every pot. To stop that, you must keep calling (or raising) with enough of your hands.

simple.title: Against a pot-size bet
simple.result: Continue with at least 50% of your range, or any bluff makes money.

simple.text: MDF = pot / (pot + bet). Small bets must be defended a lot; huge bets can be folded to more.

deeper.text: The two right-hand columns add up to 100%: MDF is just the other side of the bluffer's break-even rate.
Where MDF does not apply

items: When the bettor's range is very strong (few bluffs), folding more than MDF is correct.
When your range is capped or very weak on that board, you may simply have to fold more.
MDF ignores the cards to come: on the flop and turn, hands with equity can continue more cheaply.

deeper.text: MDF is a guide for the whole range, not a rule for each hand. It tells you how much of your range should continue, not whether this particular hand should.

examples.text: Example: defending the blinds
The button raises to 2.5 to win the 1.5 bb in the blinds. If both blinds fold more than 2.5 / (2.5 + 1.5) = 62.5% of the time together, the button profits with any two cards.

examples.title: Using this site's solver charts (and ignoring card removal)
examples.result: 47.3% is below 62.5%, so the button cannot open any two cards for profit. Part of the reason: the big blind defends 44.1% of hands.

check.why: pot / (pot + bet) = 1 / 1.5 = 67%. 33% is the share of folds the bluff needs.

check.q: A friend never bluffs on the river. Should you still defend at MDF?
options: No, fold more of your bluff catchers
check.why: MDF protects you against a player who might bluff. Against one who does not, folding more is better; that is an exploit ([[gto]]).

topics.title: Stack-to-pot ratio (SPR)
topics.short: SPR is the stack behind divided by the pot on the flop; the lower it is, the easier it is to get all-in with one pair.

simple.text: If the pot is already big compared with the money left, it takes only a bet or two to put everything in. That ratio is the **SPR**: stack behind / pot on the flop.

deeper.text: Why SPR matters

With SPR 17 there are three streets of big bets left; getting all-in with one pair means you are mostly called by two pairs and sets. With SPR 4 the stacks go in after a couple of normal bets, and an overpair or top pair top kicker is ahead of most hands willing to do that.

topics.title: Value bet
topics.short: A value bet is a bet you want called: most of the hands that call it are worse than yours.

simple.text: You bet for **value** when you expect to be called by worse hands. You are not trying to make the other player fold; you want their money.

simple.caption: Top pair, good kicker on a quiet river: weaker queens and eights may call a bet.

simple.text: The test is simple: **when called, am I ahead more than half the time?** If yes, the bet makes money. If the hands that call are mostly better, checking is better.
Before betting, name three worse hands that would call. If you cannot, it is not a value bet.

deeper.text: Why more than half

On the river, compared with checking, a bet of B wins B extra from every worse hand that calls and loses B extra to every better hand that calls. The bet gains when worse callers outnumber better callers (ignoring raises).
Thin value

A **thin** value bet is one that is ahead of the calling range only a little more than half the time, like the example below. Thin bets are where most of the money is: strong hands are easy, the medium ones decide your results.
Value on earlier streets

On the flop and turn the question is the same, but your equity against the calling range replaces "ahead or behind", and later cards can change things. Explanations on this site often say a bet **charges** draws: it makes worse hands with equity pay to see the next card ([[protection]]).
Do not bet just because you have a good hand. A strong hand on a scary board can still be behind most of the hands that call.

check.why: 12 worse against 18 better: you lose more to the better hands than you win from the worse ones. Check.

topics.title: Bluff and semi-bluff
topics.short: A bluff is a bet with a worse hand that wins when better hands fold; a semi-bluff is a bluff that can still improve.

simple.text: A **bluff** is a bet with a hand that would usually lose at showdown. It wins when the other player folds.
A **semi-bluff** is a bluff with a draw: if called, you can still hit your card. That gives you two ways to win.

simple.caption: A semi-bluff: 15 outs if called, and the pot right now if villain folds.

simple.text: A bluff needs folds: bet / (pot + bet). A half-pot bluff must work one time in three.

deeper.text: Why you must bluff sometimes

If you only bet good hands, observant players fold whenever you bet and call whenever you check. Bluffs make your bets hard to read. Solvers bluff with the hands that have the least [[showdown-value]] and the best [[blockers]].
Fold equity

**Fold equity** is the value you gain from the other player folding. A semi-bluff's EV = (folds x pot) + (calls x its value when called). Because the draw still has equity when called, it needs fewer folds than a pure bluff.
Which hands bluff

items: On the flop and turn: draws (semi-bluffs). They gain from folds and from hitting.
On the river: hands that cannot win at showdown, especially ones that do not block the hands that will fold.
Preflop: hands like A5s that block the opener's strong hands (3-bet bluffs, see [[preflop-actions]]).

deeper.text: Do not bluff with a hand that can win at showdown, such as a weak pair. It turns a hand that sometimes wins into one that only wins when better hands fold, which they rarely do.

topics.title: Bluff catcher
topics.short: A bluff catcher beats the other player's bluffs but loses to all of their value bets.

simple.text: Some hands are not strong enough to raise and not good enough to bet, but they still beat every bluff. Facing a bet, they can only win if the other player is bluffing. That is a **bluff catcher**.

simple.caption: Top pair, weak kicker after a missed diamond draw: you beat the missed draws and lose to two pair and sets.

simple.text: Whether to call depends only on one question: are there enough bluffs in their betting range to beat your [[pot-odds]]?
Bluff catcher decision: share of bluffs in their range against the equity you need. More bluffs than the price: call.

deeper.text: The balance point

A balanced bettor bluffs just often enough that your bluff catcher breaks even. For a bet of size B into a pot P, that share of bluffs is B / (P + 2B): a third for a pot-size bet, a quarter for half pot. The same formula gives the equity you need to call, so the two numbers always match.

In practice you count the combos of value and bluffs (see [[combos]]) and use your [[blockers]]: holding a card from their value hands makes calling better; holding a card from their bluffs makes it worse.
Do not call because "I have a pair". Against a range that only bets better hands, any pair is a fold.

options: It beats the bluffs but loses to all the value bets
check.why: A bluff catcher only wins against bluffs. The nuts beats everything, and a draw is a hand to bluff with, not to catch bluffs.

check.q: Villain bets pot. What share of bluffs do you need to call with a bluff catcher?
check.why: You call 1 to win 3 in total: 1 / 3 = 33%. 50% is how often a pot-size bluff must make you fold.

topics.title: Showdown value and pot control
topics.short: A hand has showdown value when it wins often enough at showdown that checking beats betting.

simple.text: Some hands are too weak to bet but good enough to win when nobody bets: middle pair, a small pocket pair, sometimes ace-high. They have **showdown value**.

simple.caption: Top pair with a ten kicker: good enough to win many showdowns, not good enough to bet into a range that calls with better queens.

simple.text: Betting these hands often makes worse hands fold and better hands call: the worst of both worlds. Checking keeps the pot small and still wins against bluffs and weaker hands.
Medium hand, quiet river: check. Bet the hands that worse hands call, and the hands that cannot win otherwise.

deeper.text: Pot control

**Pot control** means checking a medium hand on the flop or turn so the pot stays small, because the hands that would put a lot of money in are mostly better. It matters most out of position and with deep stacks ([[spr]]).
Do not turn a hand with showdown value into a bluff. If a bet is called only by better and folded by worse, you lose the pots you were winning.

options: Turned a winning hand into a losing bet
check.why: You were winning against the 20 folding hands anyway, so folding them earns nothing, and the calls lose. That is the typical mistake with showdown-value hands.

topics.title: Protection and equity denial
topics.short: Betting to make hands with some equity fold, so they cannot catch up for free.

simple.text: When you are ahead but the other player still has some chances, every free card is a small gift to them. Betting makes them either pay or fold. Folding their 25% throws away equity that was theirs: that is **denying equity**.

simple.caption: Eights against ace-king: ace-king has 6 outs and 25% equity.

simple.text: The more vulnerable your hand and the more cards can hurt you, the more you want to bet.

deeper.text: Why protection is not a separate reason

Solvers do not bet 'for protection' as such; they bet when the bet earns more than checking. But a big part of that gain often comes from folding hands that had equity. Explanations on this site say "denies equity" or "charges draws" for that.

topics.short: Small bets (a quarter to a third) for wide ranges with an edge; big bets and overbets for polarised ranges with the nuts.

topics.title: Continuation bet (c-bet)
topics.short: A c-bet is a bet on the flop by the player who made the last raise before the flop.

simple.text: You raised before the flop and the other player called. On the flop, if you bet again, that bet **continues** the story of your raise: it is a **c-bet**.

simple.caption: Ace-high flop, you opened from the button: a natural spot to c-bet small with most of your range.

simple.text: The preflop raiser usually has the stronger range, so they bet often on boards that suit it ([[range-advantage]]) and check more on boards that suit the caller.
Ask "whose board is it?" before you c-bet. High dry boards favour the raiser; low connected boards favour the caller.

deeper.text: How often and how much

items: Range advantage and dry board: bet small (a third or a quarter) very often.
Wet or middling boards: bet less often, bigger when you do, with strong hands and good draws.
Boards that favour the caller (low and connected against a button open): check more.

deeper.result: If the caller folds more than one time in four, even your worst hands profit from the bet.

deeper.text: A c-bet is not automatic. Betting every flop because you raised preflop is easy to exploit by calling and raising more.
On this site the big blind cannot lead into the preflop raiser on the flop in single-raised pots (see [[lines]]), so the flop always starts with a check from the caller.

topics.short: Check, let the other player bet, then raise: a strong move from out of position with value hands and draws.

simple.text: Out of position you act first. If you check and the other player bets, you can still raise. That is a **check-raise**. It wins more from strong hands, because the other player put money in first, and it puts big pressure on bets made with weak hands.

simple.text: When the raiser checks back the flop, its range loses many strong hands: that is when probing the turn works.

deeper.text: Why the checks matter

Each check removes hands from a range. A player who would bet their strong hands but checked back has a weaker range on the next street. The other player can then bet with more hands. Explanations on this site use "probe" for this.

When the preflop raiser (or 3-bettor) is in position, the solver's bet menu does not allow the caller to lead the flop. You will see "checks (forced)" in the hand history; it is not a decision and is not graded.
Do not barrel every street because you bet the last one. A new card changes who it favours; give up with hands that have no equity and no fold equity.

topics.title: Single-raised and 3-bet pots
topics.short: A single-raised pot had one raise and a call before the flop; a 3-bet pot had a re-raise, so it is bigger and the ranges are stronger.

simple.text: The size of the pot on the flop depends on how many raises there were before it.
In a 3-bet pot both ranges are much narrower and stronger, and the pot is already a fifth to a quarter of the stacks.
In a 3-bet pot one pair is worth more: with an [[spr]] near 4, top pair is often happy to get all-in.

deeper.text: All pot types on this site

In a 3-bet pot, the 3-bettor is the preflop aggressor and usually has the [[range-advantage]] on high boards; the caller has fewer of the very best hands, because AA and KK always 4-bet in this site's charts.
Do not play a 3-bet pot like a single-raised pot. Bets are smaller in pot terms (a quarter on the flop is common) because the pot is already big compared with the stacks.

check.q: BTN opens to 2.5, BB 3-bets to 11, BTN calls. How big is the pot?
check.why: 11 + 11 + the small blind's 0.5 = 22.5 bb. 22 forgets the dead small blind.

check.q: Why are flop bets often smaller (a quarter pot) in 3-bet pots?
options: The pot is already large compared with the stacks
check.why: With an SPR around 4, small bets already commit a good part of the stack; ranges are stronger, not weaker.

topics.title: Reading your result: grades and points
topics.short: How the site grades a decision (Best, Correct, Inaccuracy, Wrong, Blunder) and turns it into points.

simple.text: After each decision the buttons change: every option shows how often the solver takes it **with your exact two cards**, and how much it loses compared with the best one ("best" or "-1.3 bb"). Your pick is tagged **you**.

head: Grade
When
Points
rows: the solver's most frequent action, or within 5 percentage points of it
the solver takes it at least 3.5% of the time, or it costs at most 0.2% of the pot
the solver avoids it, and it loses more than 0.2% but under 1.5% of the pot
loses 6% of the pot or more

simple.text: The hand then continues along the **main line**, the same path for everyone, whatever you picked. That keeps every friend's puzzle identical and scores comparable.
Correct is a real answer, not a near-miss: the solver plays that action too, just less often. Learn most from Wrong and Blunder.

deeper.text: The exact rules

items: freq = how often the solver takes your option with your two cards; maxFreq = the highest of those.
**Best** if freq >= maxFreq - 0.05. 100 points.
**Correct** if freq >= 0.035. Points: 60 + 40 x freq / maxFreq.

**Correct** too if the option loses at most 0.2% of the pot, even when the solver rarely or never plays it: that is within the solver's own accuracy, so it counts as just as good. Same points formula, so 60 for an option the solver never takes.
Otherwise the [[ev|EV loss]] decides: loss as a percentage of the pot before you act. Over 0.2% but under 1.5%: **Inaccuracy** (40). Under 6%: **Wrong** (15). Otherwise **Blunder** (0).
Preflop chart decisions have no EV: an action the chart uses at all (but under 3.5%) is Inaccuracy, an action it never uses is Wrong.

deeper.text: Preflop frequencies come from a real solver solution, so they are rarely round: a hand can 3-bet 47.4% and call 52.6%. Postflop numbers are the solver's own mixing frequencies too. Two options that are both used a lot are both good answers ([[frequencies]]).
A puzzle's score is the average of its decisions' points, rounded. Only your **first** play counts for the leaderboard; replays are marked Practice.
What else is on the panel

items: "You chose Bet 4.1 (75% pot) · EV loss 0.3 bb (2.1% of pot)": what you did and what it cost.
**Why**: a short explanation written for this decision; underlined words link here.

**Your range** and **Villain's range**: the two ranges at this decision. Above your range, the readout starts on your exact two cards with the same percentages as the buttons (how to read it: [[reading-charts]]).

deeper.text: Do not chase the action the main line took. The main line is simply the most common path; your hand's best option can be different.

check.q: The solver bets your hand 4% and checks 96%. You bet. Grade?
check.why: 4% is above the 3.5% threshold, so it is Correct, with 60 + 40 x 0.04 / 0.96 = 62 points. It is not Best because it is far below 96%.

check.q: You picked an action the solver never takes; it loses 0.1 bb in a 20 bb pot. Grade?
check.why: 0.1 / 20 = 0.5% of the pot: more than 0.2% (which would still be Correct) but under 1.5%, so Inaccuracy, 40 points. Small EV losses are forgiven a lot.

check.why: 1.2% is under the 3.5% needed for Correct, but the chart does use the call, so it is an Inaccuracy (40 points). Wrong is for preflop actions the chart never takes.

topics.title: Reading the range chart
topics.short: Each cell is a hand class; its fill height shows how much of it is in the range and its colours show which actions it takes.

simple.text: The chart is the 13 by 13 grid from [[notation]]: pairs on the diagonal, suited hands above, offsuit hands below. Every cell stands for all the combos of one hand class.

items: **Colours** show the actions: blue fold, green check or call, red bet or raise (darker red for bigger bets).
**Width** of each colour inside a cell is how often the hand takes that action.
**Height** of the fill is how much of the hand is still in the range. A full cell: all of it. A low strip: a small part. Dark and empty: none.
Your own hand has a white outline.

simple.title: Big blind against a button open
simple.caption: AJo (row J, column A): a little under half red, a little over half green. It 3-bets 47.4% and calls 52.6%.

simple.text: The panel above the grid starts on **your two cards**, with the same numbers as the buttons. Hover or tap any cell to see that hand class instead, averaged over all its suits.

deeper.text: The readout above the grid

items: **When you do nothing** it shows your exact two cards, for example {Ah}{Jd}, labelled "your hand", with the same percentages as the action buttons.
**When you hover, focus or tap a cell** it shows that hand class, for example AJo, averaged over all its combos (12 for an offsuit hand, 4 for suited, 6 for a pair).
The two can differ for your own class: after the flop, {Ah}{Jd} and {Ac}{Js} interact with the board differently, so your exact cards can bet while the AJo average mostly checks.

deeper.text: The two bars above the grid

items: **Frequency bar**: how the whole range splits over the actions, for example Check 42%, Bet 58%. This is the range, not your hand.
**Equity bar**: your range's [[equity]] against villain's range, for example 54% against 46%. It tells you who has the [[range-advantage]].

deeper.text: Your range and villain's range

items: **Your range**: coloured by action, so you see what the solver does with every hand you could have here.
**Villain's range**: one colour, darker where more of the hand is in the range. It shows what they can have, not what they will do.
If you click a villain action in the hand history, you see villain's range coloured by its actions at that moment, and the share of the range that took the action.

deeper.text: For a first-in preflop decision every cell is full height (any hand can be dealt). Facing a 3-bet, only the hands you opened with are left, in the share you opened them. Villain's range is not shown for preflop chart decisions.
Real frequencies, not round numbers

The preflop charts are a solver solution, so cells are split in real proportions like 65% red and 35% green, not neat halves and quarters. A thin sliver of a colour means a rare action; it is still part of the strategy.
Why cells get shorter

After the flop, hands leave the range: folded preflop, folded to a bet, or blocked by board cards. A cell with a short fill means only some combos are left, for example only the suits that do not clash with the board.
Do not judge your own decision from your cell's colours: the cell is the average over all suits. The readout's default "your hand" line and the buttons show your exact cards.

topics.title: A tour of the preflop charts
topics.short: What each seat opens on this site, from 17.6% of hands under the gun to 42.7% in the small blind, and how the big blind defends.

simple.text: Before the flop the site uses fixed **charts** (in data/ranges.json) that tell each seat what to do with each of the 169 hands. They come from a real preflop solver solution (6-max, 100 bb, opens to 2.5, with rake). The rule of thumb behind all of them: **the fewer players left to act behind you, the more hands you open**.

head: Seat
Opens
Combos
simple.caption: Combos rounded to whole numbers.

simple.text: Suited hands and pairs are opened much wider than offsuit hands: they make flushes and sets, so they play well after the flop ([[remembering-ranges]] shows how to learn the charts).

deeper.text: Why the percentages look odd

You will see frequencies like 64.6% or 89.2%. They are real: at the edge of a range, a hand is almost exactly as good to open as to fold, and the solver mixes in the proportion that keeps the whole range balanced ([[frequencies]]). Hands well inside the range are 100%; mixed hands sit at the edges.
Under the gun: 17.6%

deeper.title: UTG opening chart
deeper.caption: Red raise, blue fold. A solid block of big cards and suited aces, with a ragged edge of small pairs and suited connectors.

deeper.text: Five players are left to act. Always open: pairs 77+, every suited ace from A3s (A2s 78%), suited kings to K9s, QJs to Q9s, JTs, and offsuit ATo+ and KJo+. Mixed: 66 65%, smaller pairs under 25%, K8s 89%, T9s 77%, QJo 56%, and the suited connectors 98s to 54s at 12% to 27%.
Hijack: 21.5%

deeper.title: HJ opening chart

deeper.text: One step wider: pairs 66+ (55 70%), every suited ace, suited kings to K7s (K6s and K5s almost always), Q9s+, J9s+, T9s, and offsuit ATo+, KJo+ and QJo (KTo 97%, QTo 56%). The small suited connectors stay mixed, between 28% and 50%.
Cutoff: 27.8%

deeper.title: CO opening chart

deeper.text: Pairs 44+, every suited ace, suited kings to K4s, queens to Q7s, jacks and tens to an eight (J8s, T8s), plus 98s and 97s. Offsuit: every broadway (ATo, KTo, QTo, JTo and up) and A9o; A8o 68%, A5o 50%.
Button: 41.5%

deeper.title: BTN opening chart

deeper.text: Every pair, every suited ace and every suited king; suited queens to Q3s, jacks to J5s, tens to T6s, and the connected suited hands down to 54s. Offsuit: aces to A4o, K9o+, Q9o+, J9o+, T9o; at the edge K8o 70%, T8o 56%, 98o 49%, J8o 43%.
Small blind: 42.7%, raise or fold

deeper.title: SB opening chart

deeper.text: Nearly the button's chart and a little wider: only the big blind is left behind, and the small blind already has 0.5 bb in. It adds about 21 combos of small suited and offsuit hands (64s, 85s, all K8o) and opens to 3, not 2.5. It never limps on this site.
Big blind against a button open: defend 44.1%

deeper.title: BB against a BTN open
deeper.caption: Blue fold 55.9%, green call 29.4%, red 3-bet 14.7% of all hands.

items: **Always 3-bet**: TT+, AKs, AQs, AJs, KQs, KJs, JTs, J9s, T9s, AKo and A5s. AQo 3-bets 97%.
**Close mixes**: KQo 53% 3-bet / 47% call, AJo 47% / 53%, 65s 54% / 46%.

**Call**: small pairs (44 to 22 always), the low suited kings and queens (K4s to K2s, Q4s to Q2s), A2s, and offsuit hands like A9o to A7o, ATo, KTo, QTo, JTo, Q9o and T9o, which 3-bet only now and then.
**Fold**: weak offsuit hands (A3o, K7o and below) and the worst suited ones (T2s, 94s to 92s, 83s, 82s, 72s, 62s).

deeper.text: The big blind defends so wide because it already has 1 bb in and gets a good price: it calls 1.5 to win a pot of 5.5, so it needs 1.5 / 5.5 = 27% equity before thinking about position. Being out of position means it needs a bit more in practice.
Do not expect old "standard chart" habits to hold. In this solution JTs and T9s are always 3-bets from the big blind against the button, never calls.

topics.title: How to remember preflop ranges
topics.short: Learn each range as a shape: five hand families and the boundary hand where each one stops, then quiz yourself from memory.

simple.text: Nobody remembers 169 cells and their percentages. Solver ranges have ragged edges, with hands at 23% or 71%, but their **shape** is simple. Remember a few **families** of hands and the **boundary hand** where each family stops being an always-open.

head: Family
UTG
CO
BTN
simple.caption: Hands opened 100% of the time. Just past each boundary are the mixed hands.

simple.text: Learn where each family stops. Everything stronger in that family is in; the next one or two hands below are mixes, and either choice there costs little.

deeper.text: Step 1: the five families

items: **Pairs**: they flop sets; small ones need many players folded, so they join late.
**Suited aces**: the nut flush draw, plus wheels for A5s to A2s. Even UTG opens almost all of them.
**Suited kings and broadways**: big cards that make strong top pairs and flushes.
**Suited connectors and gappers**: straights and flushes but weak pairs. They stay mixed until the cutoff and are full opens only on the button and in the small blind.
**Offsuit hands**: the family that changes most between seats. Offsuit hands need high cards, because they rarely make flushes.

deeper.text: Step 2: one shape per seat

head: Seat
Shape to remember
Boundary hands (mixed)
rows: Pairs 77+, almost every suited ace, suited broadways plus K9s and Q9s, offsuit ATo+ and KJo+
66 65%, K8s 89%, T9s 77%, QJo 56%, small pairs and suited connectors under 30%
UTG plus: 66, A2s, suited kings to K7s, J9s, QJo and nearly every KTo (97%)
Pairs 44+, suited kings to K4s, queens to Q7s, jacks and tens to an eight; every offsuit broadway and A9o
Every pair, every suited ace and king, suited queens to Q3s; offsuit A4o+ and every two cards nine or higher
The button's shape, a little wider at the bottom: all of K8o, plus 64s and 85s

deeper.text: Step 3: see how the ranges grow
Each later seat keeps the earlier range and adds a layer. In this solution no hand is opened less often from a later seat up to the button, so seeing only the layer is enough.

deeper.title: What the cutoff adds to UTG (135 combos)
deeper.caption: Darker cells are added more fully: the small pairs, the rest of the suited kings and queens, the suited connectors, and the offsuit broadways from KTo down.

deeper.title: What the button adds to the cutoff (182 combos)
deeper.caption: The bottom of the suited kings, queens and jacks, the small suited connectors, and a big block of offsuit aces and offsuit hands nine and higher.

deeper.text: Step 4: practise by recalling, not rereading

items: Cover the chart. For each seat, write the boundary hand of each family (the tables above are the answer key). Check against the real chart and mark every miss.
Repeat the same drill tomorrow, in three days and in a week. Spaced repeats beat one long session.
Mix the seats: deal yourself random hands from a real deck and a random seat, say "open", "fold" or "mix" out loud, then check. Twenty hands take three minutes.
Play this site's puzzles: every preflop decision is a free quiz against the chart.

deeper.text: Do not try to memorise exact mixing percentages like 64.6%. Know which side of the boundary a hand is on; for a hand near the boundary, either choice loses very little, and the site grades frequent mixes as Correct or Best.

examples.text: Example: is the hand in?
Cutoff, {Kd}{7d}. Family: suited kings. Cutoff boundary: K4s. K7s is stronger, so it always opens.
UTG, {Ah}{Jc}. Family: offsuit aces. UTG boundary: ATo. AJo is stronger, so it opens.
UTG, {6s}{6c}. Family: pairs. UTG boundary: 77. 66 is just below it, a mixed hand (65%): opening or folding are both reasonable.
Your turn

Button, {Qc}{9d}. Family? Boundary? In or out? (Answer: offsuit hands with both cards nine or higher are always in on the button, so Q9o opens.) Then: small blind, {Ks}{8h}? (Answer: the small blind opens every K8o; the button only 70%.)

check.q: What is the weakest pocket pair UTG always opens on this site?
check.why: UTG opens 77 and up every time; 66 is a mix (65%) and the smaller pairs are opened rarely. 22 is an always-open only on the button and in the small blind.

check.q: Which is the first seat that opens every offsuit broadway (ATo, KTo, QTo, JTo and up)?
check.why: The cutoff opens all offsuit broadways. The hijack opens QTo 56% and JTo 18%; UTG opens KTo only 31%.

check.q: Best way to learn the charts?
options: Cover them and recall the boundary hands, spaced over days, mixing seats
check.why: Recalling from memory (retrieval practice), spread over days and mixed between seats, gives far better long-term memory than rereading. Exact percentages matter little near a boundary.
